newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar tumbles against yen in Tokyo on trade fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar tumbles against yen in Tokyo on trade fears.

text.p: Trade friction fears, expectations of a shrinking U.S.-Japan interest rate gap and worries over the future of Europe's single currency sliced more than two yen off the dollar's value on Monday before it bounced back a bit.

The dollar fell as low as 111.80 yen in Asian trade -- its lowest level since November 25, 1996 -- before recovering to stand at about 112.68 yen by late Tokyo afternoon. The greenback closed at about 114.38 yen on Friday in New York.
Some analysts said the dollar might stabilise around its current levels for now, but others argued it could slide below the critical 110 yen barrier in the short-term.

The dollar's sharp morning slide prompted only muted comments from Japanese officials, leading dealers to bet that Tokyo will tolerate a yen rise to around 110 yen to the dollar ahead of a Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver on June 20-22.

"Stability of currency rates...will contribute to a self-sustainable economic recovery," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary panel, adding that he would do his best to achieve such stability.

The sentiment was echoed by vice trade minister Tsutomu Makino, who told reporters: "Wild currency moves are not desirable." Makino, doubtless reflecting the potentially negative impact of the yen's recent rise on Japanese exporters, dubbed the currency's movement "excessive".
But other officials shied away from that term, and Tokyo's "Mr Yen", the Finance Ministry's Eisuke Sakakibara, was uncharacteristically silent when queried about currency moves.

The looming Denver summit and comments by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Friday have refocused attention on a likely rise in Japan's trade surplus and the potential for more trade friction with Washington as a result.

"The concern we have right now is that we see an upturn in Japan's trade surplus with us and at the same time we see a downturn in some of our major exports, for example, vehicles," Barshefsky said in Washington.
Reports that Japan's growing trade surplus will be on the agenda at the Denver summit have also made the market jittery.
"This time the market focus is the Japanese trade surplus," said Hideki Naito, an analyst at MMS Standard and Poor's.

Japan will announce its current account data for April on Wednesday. Economists expect to see a substantial rise in the surplus, given a drop in imports due to sluggish domestic demand after an April 1 consumption tax increase.

A Reuters poll of economists showed, on average, that the April current account surplus would grow to 1.13 trillion yen ($10.0 billion), compared with a surplus of 566.6 billion yen ($5.05 billion) last year.
The forecasts ranged from 990 billion yen ($8.83 billion) to 1.21 trillion yen ($10.8 billion).

Currency traders said early dollar selling on Monday was led by overseas speculators who had bought too many dollars in recent months on expectations that the wide gap between U.S. and Japanese interest rates would persist.

But market players are now sensing a possible narrowing of that gap, given their fading expectations of a U.S. credit tightening in July. "What we are seeing now is the liquidation of these long dollar positions," said Chris Pavlov, treasurer at Midland Bank.
Uncertainty over the future of the single European currency also helped undermine the dollar by prompting a spate of yen purchases against the mark and other European currencies.
Pavlov said the dollar could stabilise at around 111-112 yen, but others said the U.S. currency could easily fall to 110 yen -- maybe even lower.

"The dollar is indeed at a critical level and...we're certainly looking at the 108 level to be the near-term level to be tested. But depending on the rate of yen buying, that could even accelerate further," said Edwin Sarfo, an options strategist at IDEA in Tokyo.
